entries.ef70b43d1550e6e8d363dde1ba3d3e6346d84508: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14"/><title type="x-ms">Second Samuel</title> <div sID="gen5940" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5941" type="x-p"/> This book is the history of the reign of king David. We had in the foregoing book an account of his designation to the government, and his struggles with Saul, which ended at length in the death of his persecutor. This book begins with his accession to the throne, and is entirely taken up with the affairs of the government during the forty years he reigned, and therefore is entitled by the LXX. <hi type="italic">The Third Book of the Kings.</hi> It gives us an account of David's triumphs and his troubles. I. His triumphs over the house of Saul (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.1-2Sam.4.12">ch. i.-iv.</reference>), over the Jebusites and Philistines (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.1-2Sam.5.25">ch. v.</reference>), at the bringing up of the ark (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.1-2Sam.7.29">ch. vi. and vii.</reference>), over the neighbouring nations that opposed him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.1-2Sam.10.19">ch. viii.-x.</reference>); and so far the history is agreeable to what we might expect from David's character and the choice made of him. But his cloud has a dark side. II. We have his troubles, the causes of them, his sin in the matter of Uriah (<reference osisRef="2Sam.11.1-2Sam.12.31">ch. xi. and xii.</reference>), the troubles themselves from the sin of Amnon (<reference osisRef="2Sam.13.1-2Sam.13.39">ch. xiii.</reference>), the rebellion of Absalom (<reference osisRef="2Sam.14.1-2Sam.14.43">ch. xiv.-xix.</reference>) and of Sheba (<reference osisRef="2Sam.20.1-2Sam.20.26">ch. xx.</reference>), and the plague in Israel for his numbering the people (<reference osisRef="2Sam.24.1-2Sam.24.25">ch. xxiv.</reference>), besides the famine of the Gibeonites, <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.1-2Sam.21.22">ch. xxi</reference>. His son we have (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.1-2Sam.22.51">ch. xxii.</reference>), and his words and worthies, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.1-2Sam.23.39">ch. xxiii</reference>. Many things in his history are very instructive; but for the hero who is the subject of it, though in many instances he appears here very great, and very good, and very much the favourite of heaven, yet it must be confessed that his honour shines brighter in his Psalms than in his Annals. <div eID="gen5941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5942" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5943" type="x-p"/> In the close of the foregoing book (with which this is connected as a continuation of the same history) we had Saul's exit; he went down slain to the pit, though he was the terror of the mighty in the land of the living. We are now to look towards the rising sun, and to enquire where David is, and what he is doing. In this chapter we have, I. Tidings brought him to Ziklag of the death of Saul and Jonathan, by an Amalekite, who undertook to give him a particular narrative of it, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.1-2Sam.1.10">ver. 1-10</reference>. II. David's sorrowful reception of these tidings, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.11-2Sam.1.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>. III. Justice done upon the messenger, who boasted that he had helped Saul to dispatch himself, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.13-2Sam.1.16">ver. 13-16</reference>. IV. An elegy which David penned upon this occasion, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.17-2Sam.1.27">ver. 17-27</reference>. And in all this David's breast appears very happily free from the sparks both of revenge and ambition, and he observes a very suitable demeanour. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14"/> <div eID="gen5943" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5942" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Concern at Saul's Fate. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1055.)</title> <div sID="gen5944" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now it came to pass after the death of Saul, when David was returned from the slaughter of the Amalekites, and David had abode two days in Ziklag; <hi type="super">2</hi> It came even to pass on the third day, that, behold, a man came out of the camp from Saul with his clothes rent, and earth upon his head: and <hi type="italic">so</hi> it was, when he came to David, that he fell to the earth, and did obeisance. <hi type="super">3</hi> And David said unto him, From whence comest thou? And he said unto him, Out of the camp of Israel am I escaped. <hi type="super">4</hi> And David said unto him, How went the matter? I pray thee, tell me. And he answered, That the people are fled from the battle, and many of the people also are fallen and dead; and Saul and Jonathan his son are dead also. <hi type="super">5</hi> And David said unto the young man that told him, How knowest thou that Saul and Jonathan his son be dead? <hi type="super">6</hi> And the young man that told him said, As I happened by chance upon mount Gilboa, behold, Saul leaned upon his spear; and, lo, the chariots and horsemen followed hard after him. <hi type="super">7</hi> And when he looked behind him, he saw me, and called unto me. And I answered, Here <hi type="italic">am</hi> I. <hi type="super">8</hi> And he said unto me, Who <hi type="italic">art</hi> thou? And I answered him, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> an Amalekite. <hi type="super">9</hi> He said unto me again, Stand, I pray thee, upon me, and slay me: for anguish is come upon me, because my life <hi type="italic">is</hi> yet whole in me. <hi type="super">10</hi> So I stood upon him, and slew him, because I was sure that he could not live after that he was fallen: and I took the crown that <hi type="italic">was</hi> upon his head, and the bracelet that <hi type="italic">was</hi> on his arm, and have brought them hither unto my lord. <div eID="gen5944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5945" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. David settling again in Ziklag, his own city, after he had rescued his family and friends out of the hands of the Amalekites (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.1">v. 1</reference>): He <hi type="italic">abode in Ziklag.</hi> Thence he was now sending presents to his friends (<reference osisRef="1Sam.30.26">1 Sam. xxx. 26</reference>), and there he was ready to receive those that came into his interests; not men in distress and debt, as his first followers were, but persons of quality in their country, <hi type="italic">mighty men, men of war,</hi> and <hi type="italic">captains of thousands</hi> (as we find, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.1">1 Chron. xii. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.8">8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.20">20</reference>); such came day by day to him, God stirring up their hearts to do so, till he had a <hi type="italic">great host, like the host of God,</hi> as it is said, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.22">1 Chron. xii. 22</reference>. The secret springs of revolutions are unaccountable, and must be resolved into that Providence which turns all hearts as the rivers of water. <div eID="gen5945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5946" type="x-p"/> II. Intelligence brought him thither of the death of Saul. It was strange that he did not leave some spies about the camp, to bring him early notice of the issue of the engagement, a sign that he desired not Saul's woeful day, nor was impatient to come to the throne, but willing to wait till those tidings were brought to him which many a one would have sent more than half-way to meet. He that believes does not make haste, takes good news when it comes and is not uneasy while it is in the coming. 1. The messenger presents himself to David as an express, in the posture of a mourner for the deceased prince and a subject to the succeeding one. He came with his clothes rent, and made obeisance to David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.2">v. 2</reference>), pleasing himself with the fancy that he had the honour to be the first that did him homage as his sovereign, but it proved he was the first that received from him sentence of death as his judge. He told David he came from the camp of Israel, and intimated the bad posture it was in when he said he had escaped out of it, having much ado to get away with his life, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.3">v. 3</reference>. 2. He gives him a general account of the issue of the battle. David was very desirous to know how the matter went, as one that had more reason than any to be concerned for the public; and he told him very distinctly that the army of Israel was routed, many slain, and, among the rest, Saul and Jonathan, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.4">v. 4</reference>. He named only Saul and Jonathan, because he knew David would be most solicitous to know their fate; for Saul was the man whom he most feared and Jonathan the man whom he most loved. 3. He gives him a more particular account of the death of Saul. It is probable that David had heard, by the report of others, what the issue of the war was, for multitudes resorted to him, it should seem, in consequence; but he was desirous to know the certainty of the report concerning Saul and Jonathan, either because he was not forward to believe it or because he would not proceed upon it to make his own claims till he was fully assured of it. He therefore asks, <hi type="italic">How knowest thou that Saul and Jonathan are dead?</hi> in answer to which the young man tells him a very ready story, putting it past doubt that Saul was dead, for he himself had been not only an eye-witness of his death, but an instrument of it, and therefore David might rely upon his testimony. He says nothing, in his narrative, of the death of Jonathan, knowing how ungrateful that would be to David, but accounts only for Saul, thinking (as David understood it well enough, <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.10">ch. iv. 10</reference>) that he should be welcome for that, and rewarded as one that brought good tidings. The account he gives of this matter is, (1.) Very particular. That he happened to go to the place where Saul was (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.6">v. 6</reference>) as a passenger, not as a soldier, and therefore an indifferent person, that he found Saul endeavouring to run himself through with his own spear, none of his attendants being willing to do it for him; and, it seems, he could not do it dexterously for himself: his hand and heart failed him. The miserable man had not courage enough either to live or die; he therefore called this stranger to him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.7">v. 7</reference>), enquired what countryman he was, for, provided he was not a Philistine, he would gladly receive from his hand the <hi type="italic">coup de grace</hi> (as the French call it concerning those that are broken on the wheel)—<hi type="italic">the merciful stroke,</hi> that might dispatch him out of his pain. Understanding that he was an Amalekite (neither one of his subjects nor one of his enemies), he begs this favour from him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Stand upon me, and slay me.</hi> He is now sick of his dignity and willing to be trampled upon, sick of his life and willing to be slain. Who then would be inordinately fond of life or honour? The case may he such, even with those that have no hope in their death, that yet they may <hi type="italic">desire to die, and death flee from them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.9.6">Rev. ix. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">Anguish has come upon me;</hi> so we read it, as a complaint of the pain and terror his spirit was seized with. If his conscience now brought to mind the javelin he had cast at David, his pride, malice, and perfidiousness, and especially the murder of the priests, no marvel that anguish came upon him: moles (they say) open their eyes when they are dying. Sense of unpardoned guilt will make death indeed the king of terrors. Those that have baffled their convictions will perhaps, in their dying moments, be overpowered by them. The margin reads it as a complaint of the inconvenience of his clothes; that his coat of mail which he had for defence, or his embroidered coat which he had for ornament, hindered him, that he could not get the spear far enough into his body, or so straitened him, now that his body swelled with anguish, that he could not expire. Let no man's clothes be his pride, for it may so happen that they may be his burden and snare. "Hereupon," saith our young man, "<hi type="italic">I stood upon him, and slew him</hi>" (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.10">v. 10</reference>) at which word, perhaps, he observed David look upon him with some show of displeasure, and therefore he excuses himself in the next words: "<hi type="italic">For I was sure he could not live;</hi> his life was whole in him indeed, but he would certainly have fallen into the hands of the Philistines or given himself another thrust." (2.) It is doubtful whether this story be true. If it be, the righteousness of God is to be observed, that Saul, who spared the Amalekites in contempt of the divine command, received his death's wound from an Amalekite. But most interpreters think that it was false, and that, though he might happen to be present, yet he was not assisting in the death of Saul, but told David so in expectation that he would reward him for it, as having done him a piece of good service. Those who would rejoice at the fall of an enemy are apt to measure others by themselves, and to think that they will do so too. But a man after God's own heart is not to be judged of by common men. I am not clear whether this young man's story was true or no: it may consist with the narrative in the chapter before, and be an addition to it, as Peter's account of the death of Judas (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.18">Acts i. 18</reference>) is to the narrative, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.5">Matt. xxvii. 5</reference>. What is there called <hi type="italic">a sword</hi> may here be called <hi type="italic">a spear,</hi> or when he fell upon his sword he leaned on his spear. (3.) However he produced that which was proof sufficient of the death of Saul, the crown that was upon his head and the bracelet that was on his arm. It should seem Saul was so foolishly fond of these as to wear them in the field of battle, which made him a fair mark for the archers, by distinguishing him from those about him; but as <hi type="italic">pride</hi> (we say) <hi type="italic">feels no cold,</hi> so it fears no danger, from that which gratifies it. These fell into the hands of this Amalekite. Saul spared the best of their spoil, and now the best of his came to one of that devoted nation. He brought them to David, as the rightful owner of them now that Saul was dead, not doubting but by his officiousness herein to recommend himself to the best preferments in his court or camp. The tradition of the Jews is that this Amalekite was the son of Doeg (for the Amalekites were descendants from Edom), and that Doeg, who they suppose was Saul's armour-bearer, before he slew himself gave Saul's crown and bracelet (the ensigns of his royalty) to his son, and bade him carry them to David, to curry favour with him. But this is a groundless conceit. Doeg's son, it is likely, was so well known to Saul that he needed not ask him as he did this Amalekite (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.8">v. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">Who art thou?</hi> David had been long waiting for the crown, and now it was brought to him by an Amalekite. See how God can serve his own purposes of kindness to his people, even by designing (ill-designing) men, who aim at nothing but to set up themselves.
entries.938cb0369776d41c5254331032e6f18c8b65f6b5: <div eID="gen5946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5947" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Then David took hold on his clothes, and rent them; and likewise all the men that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him: <hi type="super">12</hi> And they mourned, and wept, and fasted until even, for Saul, and for Jonathan his son, and for the people of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and for the house of Israel; because they were fallen by the sword. <hi type="super">13</hi> And David said unto the young man that told him, Whence <hi type="italic">art</hi> thou? And he answered, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the son of a stranger, an Amalekite. <hi type="super">14</hi> And David said unto him, How wast thou not afraid to stretch forth thine hand to destroy the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's anointed? <hi type="super">15</hi> And David called one of the young men, and said, Go near, <hi type="italic">and</hi> fall upon him. And he smote him that he died. <hi type="super">16</hi> And David said unto him, Thy blood <hi type="italic">be</hi> upon thy head; for thy mouth hath testified against thee, saying, I have slain the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's anointed. <div eID="gen5947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5948" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. David's reception of these tidings. So far was he from falling into a transport of joy, as the Amalekite expected, that he fell into a passion of weeping, <hi type="italic">rent his clothes</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.11">v. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">mourned and fasted</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.12">v. 12</reference>), not only for his people Israel and Jonathan his friend but for Saul his enemy. This he did, not only as a man of honour, in observance of that decorum which forbids us to insult over those that are fallen, and requires us to attend our relations to the grave with respect, whatever we lost by their life or got by their death, but as a good man and a man of conscience, that had forgiven the injuries Saul had done him and bore him no malice. He knew it, before his son wrote it (<reference osisRef="Prov.24.17-Prov.24.18">Prov. xxiv. 17, 18</reference>), that if we <hi type="italic">rejoice when our enemy falls the Lord sees it, and it displeases him;</hi> and that <hi type="italic">he who is glad at calamities shall not go unpunished,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.5">Prov. xvii. 5</reference>. By this it appears that those passages in David's psalms which express his desire of, and triumph in, the ruin of his enemies, proceeded not from a spirit of revenge, nor any irregular passion, but from a holy zeal for the glory of God and the public good; for by what he did here, when he heard of Saul's death, we may perceive that his natural temper was very tender, and that he was kindly affected even to those that hated him. He was very sincere, no question, in his mourning for Saul, and it was not pretended, or a copy of his countenance only. His passion was so strong, on this occasion, that it moved those about him; <hi type="italic">all that were with him,</hi> at least in complaisance to him, <hi type="italic">rent their clothes,</hi> and they <hi type="italic">fasted till even,</hi> in token of their sorrow; and probably it was a religious fast: they humbled themselves under the hand of God, and prayed for the repairing of the breaches made upon Israel by this defeat. <div eID="gen5948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5949" type="x-p"/> II. The reward he gave to him that brought him the tidings. Instead of preferring him, he put him to death, judged him out of his own mouth, as a murderer of his prince, and ordered him to be forthwith executed for the same. What a surprise was this to the messenger, who thought he should have favour shown him for his pains. In vain did he plead that he had Saul's order for it, that it was a real kindness to him, that he must inevitably have died; all those pleas are overruled: "<hi type="italic">Thy mouth has testified against thee, saying, I have slain the Lord's anointed</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.16">v. 16</reference>), therefore thou must die." Now, <div eID="gen5949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5950" type="x-p"/> 1. David herein did not do unjustly. For, (1.) The man was an Amalekite. This, lest he should have mistaken it in his narrative, he made him own a second time, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.13">v. 13</reference>. That nation, and all that belonged to it, were doomed to destruction, so that, in slaying him, David did what his predecessor should have done and was rejected for not doing. (2.) He did himself confess the crime, so that the evidence was, by the consent of all laws, sufficient to convict him; for every man is presumed to make the best of himself. If he did as he said, he deserved to die for treason (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.14">v. 14</reference>), doing that which, it is probable, he heard Saul's own armour-bearer refuse to do; if not, yet by boasting that he had done it he plainly showed that if there had been occasion he would have done it, and would have made nothing of it; and, by boasting of it to David, he showed what opinion he had of him, that he would rejoice in it, as one altogether like himself, which was an intolerable affront to him who had himself once and again refused to <hi type="italic">stretch forth his hand against the Lord's anointed.</hi> And his lying to David, if indeed it was a lie, was highly criminal, and proved, as sooner or later that sin will prove, lying against his own head. <div eID="gen5950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5951" type="x-p"/> 2. He did honourably and well. Hereby he demonstrated the sincerity of his grief, discouraged all others from thinking by doing the like to ingratiate themselves with him, and did that which might probably oblige the house of Saul and win upon them, and recommend him to the people as one that was zealous for public justice, without regard to his own private interest. We may learn from it that to give assistance to any in murdering themselves, directly or indirectly, if done wittingly, incurs the guilt of blood, and that the lives of princes ought to be, in a special manner, precious to us.
entries.544f858af5bf14692591f5ddbf75e86b309b210b: <div eID="gen5951" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Lamentation for Jonathan. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1055.)</title> <div sID="gen5952" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> And David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and over Jonathan his son: <hi type="super">18</hi> (Also he bade them teach the children of Judah <hi type="italic">the use of</hi> the bow: behold, <hi type="italic">it is</hi> written in the book of Jasher.) <hi type="super">19</hi> The beauty of Israel is slain upon thy high places: how are the mighty fallen! <hi type="super">20</hi> Tell <hi type="italic">it</hi> not in Gath, publish <hi type="italic">it</hi> not in the streets of Askelon; lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised triumph. <hi type="super">21</hi> Ye mountains of Gilboa, <hi type="italic">let there be</hi> no dew, neither <hi type="italic">let there be</hi> rain, upon you, nor fields of offerings: for there the shield of the mighty is vilely cast away, the shield of Saul, <hi type="italic">as though he had</hi> not <hi type="italic">been</hi> anointed with oil. <hi type="super">22</hi> From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, the bow of Jonathan turned not back, and the sword of Saul returned not empty. <hi type="super">23</hi> Saul and Jonathan <hi type="italic">were</hi> lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided: they were swifter than eagles, they were stronger than lions. <hi type="super">24</hi> Ye daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you in scarlet, with <hi type="italic">other</hi> delights, who put on ornaments of gold upon your apparel. <hi type="super">25</hi> How are the mighty fallen in the midst of the battle! O Jonathan, <hi type="italic">thou wast</hi> slain in thine high places. <hi type="super">26</hi> I am distressed for thee, my brother Jonathan: very pleasant hast thou been unto me: thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women. <hi type="super">27</hi> How are the mighty fallen, and the weapons of war perished! <div eID="gen5952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5953" type="x-p"/> When David had rent his clothes, mourned, and wept, and fasted, for the death of Saul, and done justice upon him who made himself guilty of it, one would think he had made full payment of the debt of honour he owed to his memory; yet this is not all: we have here a poem he wrote on that occasion; for he was a great master of his pen as well as of his sword. By this elegy he designed both to express his own sorrow for this great calamity and to impress the like on the minds of others, who ought to lay it to heart. The putting of lamentations into poems made them, 1. The more moving and affecting. The passion of the poet, or singer, is, by this way, wonderfully communicated to the readers and hearers. 2. The more lasting. Thus they were made, not only to spread far, but to continue long, from generation to generation. Those might gain information by poems that would not read history. Here we have, <div eID="gen5953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5954" type="x-p"/> I. The orders David gave with this elegy (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">He bade them teach the children of Judah</hi> (his own tribe, whatever others did) <hi type="italic">the use of the bow,</hi> either. 1. The bow used in war. Not but that the children of Judah knew how to use the bow (it was so commonly used in war, long before this, that the sword and bow were put for all weapons of war, <reference osisRef="Gen.48.22">Gen. xlviii. 22</reference>), but perhaps they had of late made more use of slings, as David in killing Goliath, because cheaper, and David would have them now to see the inconvenience of these (for it was the archers of the Philistines that bore so hard upon Saul, <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.3">1 Sam. xxi. 3</reference>), and to return more generally to the use of the bow, to exercise themselves in this weapon, that they might be in a capacity to avenge the death of their prince upon the Philistines, and to outdo them at their own weapon. It was a pity but those that had such good heads and hearts as the children of Judah should be well armed. David hereby showed his authority over and concern for the armies of Israel, and set himself to rectify the errors of the former reign. But we find that the companies which had now come to David to Ziklag were armed with bows (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.2">1 Chron. xii. 2</reference>); therefore, 2. Some understand it either of some musical instrument called <hi type="italic">a bow</hi> (to which he would have the mournful ditties sung) or of the elegy itself: <hi type="italic">He bade them teach the children of Judah Kesheth, the bow,</hi> that is, this song, which was so entitled for the sake of Jonathan's bow, the achievements of which are here celebrated. Moses commanded Israel to learn his song (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.19">Deut. xxxi. 19</reference>), so David his. Probably he bade the Levites teach them. It is <hi type="italic">written in the book of Jasher,</hi> there it was kept upon record, and thence transcribed into this history. That book was probably a collection of state-poems; what is said to be written in that book (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.13">Josh. x. 13</reference>) is also poetical, a fragment of an historical poem. Even songs would be forgotten and lost if they were not committed to writing, that best conservatory of knowledge. <div eID="gen5954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5955" type="x-p"/> II. The elegy itself. It is not a divine hymn, nor given by inspiration of God to be used in divine service, nor is there any mention of God in it; but it is a human composition, and therefore was inserted, not in the book of Psalms (which, being of divine original, is preserved), but in the book of Jasher, which, being only a collection of common poems, is long since lost. This elegy proves David to have been, <div eID="gen5955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5956" type="x-p"/> 1. A man of an excellent spirit, in four things:— <div eID="gen5956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5957" type="x-p"/> (1.) He was very generous to Saul, his sworn enemy. Saul was his father-in-law, his sovereign, and the anointed of the Lord; and therefore, though he had done him a great deal of wrong, David does not wreak his revenge upon his memory when he is in his grave; but like a good man, and a man of honour, [1.] He conceals his faults; and, though there was no preventing their appearance in his history, yet they should not appear in this elegy. Charity teaches us to make the best we can of every body and to say nothing of those of whom we can say no good, especially when they are gone. <hi type="italic">De mortuis nil nisi bonum</hi>—<hi type="italic">Say nothing but good concerning the dead.</hi> We ought to deny ourselves the satisfaction of making personal reflections upon those who have been injurious to us, much more drawing their character thence, as if every man must of necessity be a bad man that has done ill by us. Let the corrupt part of the memory be buried with the corrupt part of the man—earth to earth, ashes to ashes; let the blemish be hidden and a veil drawn over the deformity. [2.] He celebrates that which was praiseworthy in him. He does not commend him for that which he was not, says nothing of his piety or fidelity. Those funeral commendations which are gathered out of the spoils of truth are not at all to the praise of those on whom they are bestowed, but very much the dispraise of those who unjustly misplace them. But he has this to say in honour of Saul himself, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That he was <hi type="italic">anointed with oil</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.21">v. 21</reference>), the sacred oil, which signified his elevation to, and qualification for, the government. Whatever he was otherwise, the <hi type="italic">crown of the anointing oil of his God was upon him,</hi> as is said of the high priest (<reference osisRef="Lev.21.12">Lev. xxi. 12</reference>), and on that account he was to be honoured, because God, the fountain of honour, had honoured him. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That he was a man of war, a <hi type="italic">mighty man</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.19-2Sam.1.21">v. 19-21</reference>), that he had often been victorious over the enemies of Israel and <hi type="italic">vexed them whithersoever he turned,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.47">1 Sam. xiv. 47</reference>. His <hi type="italic">sword returned not empty,</hi> but satiated with blood and spoil, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.22">v. 22</reference>. His disgrace and fall at last must not make his former successes and services to be forgotten. Though his sun set under a cloud, time was when it shone brightly. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> That take him with Jonathan he was a man of a very agreeable temper, that recommended himself to the affections of his subjects (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant.</hi> Jonathan was always so, and Saul was so as long as he concurred with him. Take them together, and in the pursuit of the enemy, never were men more bold, more brave; they were <hi type="italic">swifter than eagles and stronger than lions.</hi> Observe, Those that were most fierce and fiery in the camp were no less sweet and lovely in the court, as amiable to the subject as they were formidable to the foe; a rare combination of softness and sharpness they had, which makes any man's temper very happy. It may be understood of the harmony and affection that for the most part subsisted between Saul and Jonathan: they were lovely and pleasant one to another, Jonathan a dutiful son, Saul an affectionate father; and therefore dear to each other in their lives, and <hi type="italic">in their death they were not divided,</hi> but kept close together in the stand they made against the Philistines, and fell together in the same cause. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> That he had enriched his country with the spoils of conquered nations, and introduced a more splendid attire. When they had a king like the nations, they must have clothes like the nations; and herein he was, in a particular manner, obliging to his female subjects, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.24">v. 24</reference>. The <hi type="italic">daughters of Israel</hi> he <hi type="italic">clothed in scarlet,</hi> which was their delight. <div eID="gen5957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5958" type="x-p"/> (2.) He was very grateful to Jonathan, his sworn friend. Besides the tears he shed over him, and the encomiums he gives of him in common with Saul, he mentions him with some marks of distinction (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">O Jonathan! thou wast slain in thy high places!</hi> which (compared with <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.19">v. 19</reference>) intimates that he meant him by <hi type="italic">the beauty of Israel,</hi> which, he there says, was slain upon the high places. He laments Jonathan as his particular friend (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">My brother, Jonathan;</hi> not so much because of what he would have been to him if he had lived, very serviceable no doubt in his advancement to the throne and instrumental to prevent those long struggles which, for want of his assistance, he had with the house of Saul (had this been the only ground of his grief it would have been selfish), but he lamented him for what he had been: "<hi type="italic">Very pleasant hast thou been unto me;</hi> but that pleasantness is now over, and <hi type="italic">I am distressed for thee.</hi>" He had reason to say that Jonathan's love to him was wonderful; surely never was the like, for a man to love one who he knew was to take the crown over his head, and to be so faithful to his rival: this far surpassed the highest degree of conjugal affection and constancy. See here, [1.] That nothing is more delightful in this world than a true friend, that is wise and good, that kindly receives and returns our affection, and is faithful to us in all our true interests. [2.] That nothing is more distressful than the loss of such a friend; it is parting with a piece of one's self. It is the vanity of this world that what is most pleasant to us we are most liable to be distressed in. The more we love the more we grieve. <div eID="gen5958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5959" type="x-p"/> (3.) He was deeply concerned for the honour of God; for this is what he has an eye to when he fears lest <hi type="italic">the daughters of the uncircumcised,</hi> that are out of covenant with God, should triumph over Israel, and the God of Israel, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.20">v. 20</reference>. Good men are touched in a very sensible part by the reproaches of those that reproach God. <div eID="gen5959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5960" type="x-p"/> (4.) He was deeply concerned for the public welfare. It was the beauty of Israel that was slain (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.19">v. 19</reference>) and the honour of the public that was disgraced: The <hi type="italic">mighty have fallen</hi> (this is three times lamented, (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.19">v. 19</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.25">25</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.27">27</reference>), and so the strength of the people is weakened. Public losses are most laid to heart by men of public spirit. David hoped God would make him instrumental to repair those losses and yet laments them. <div eID="gen5960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5961" type="x-p"/> 2. A man of a fine imagination, as well as a wise and holy man. The expressions are all excellent, and calculated to work upon the passions. (1.) The embargo he would fain lay upon Fame is elegant (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">Tell it not in Gath.</hi> It grieved him to the heart to think that it would be proclaimed in the cities of the Philistines, and that they would insult over Israel upon it, and the more in remembrance of the triumphs of Israel over them formerly, when they sang, <hi type="italic">Saul has slain his thousands;</hi> for this would now be retorted. (2.) The curse he entails on the mountains of Gilboa, the theatre on which this tragedy was acted: <hi type="italic">Let there be no dew upon you, nor fields of offerings,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.21">v. 21</reference>. This is a poetical strain, like that of Job, <hi type="italic">Let the day perish wherein I was born.</hi> Not as if David wished that any part of the land of Israel might be barren, but, to express his sorrow for the thing, he speaks with a seeming indignation at the place. Observe, [1.] How the fruitfulness of the earth depends upon heaven. The worst thing he could wish to the mountains of Gilboa was barrenness and unprofitableness to man: those are miserable that are useless. It was the curse Christ pronounced on the fig-tree, <hi type="italic">Never fruit grow on thee more,</hi> and that took effect—the fig-tree withered away: this, on the mountains of Gilboa, did not. But, when he wished them barren, he wished there might be no rain upon them; and, if the heavens be brass, the earth will soon be iron. [2.] How the fruitfulness of the earth must therefore be devoted to heaven, which is intimated in his calling the fruitful fields <hi type="italic">fields of offerings.</hi> Those fruits of their land that were offered to God were the crown and glory of it: and therefore the failure of the offerings is the saddest consequent of the failure of the corn. See <reference osisRef="Joel.1.9">Joel i. 9</reference>. To want that wherewith we should honour God is worse than to want that wherewith we should sustain ourselves. This is the reproach David fastens upon the mountains of Gilboa, which, having been stained with royal blood, thereby forfeited celestial dews. In this elegy Saul had a more honourable interment than that which the men of Jabesh-Gilead gave him.  <chapter eID="2Sam.1"/> <div eID="gen5961" type="x-p"/>

entries.5747ced1ec0c1d33ed847f6f2b146cfe1dcc5464: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2825"/><title type="x-ms">THE SECOND BOOK OF SAMUEL, OTHERWISE CALLED THE SECOND BOOK OF THE KINGS.</title> <div sID="gen3878" type="x-p"/> Commentary by Robert Jamieson<div eID="gen3878" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <div sID="gen3879" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.1-2Sam.1.16">2Sa 1:1-16</reference>. An Amalekite Brings Tidings of Saul's Death.<div eID="gen3879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3880" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2825"/><hi type="bold">1. David had abode two days in Ziklag--</hi>Though greatly reduced by the Amalekite incendiaries, that town was not so completely sacked and destroyed, but David and his six hundred followers, with their families, could still find some accommodation. <div eID="gen3880" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a7edbf48e9a993d2c4433aa1f3b119b2a2c54d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2826"/><div sID="gen3881" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2826"/><hi type="bold">2-12. a man came out of the camp from Saul--</hi>As the narrative of Saul's death, given in the last chapter, is inspired, it must be considered the true account, and the Amalekite's story a fiction of his own, invented to ingratiate himself with David, the presumptive successor to the throne. David's question, "How went the matter?" evinces the deep interest he took in the war, an interest that sprang from feelings of high and generous patriotism, not from views of ambition. The Amalekite, however, judging him to be actuated by a selfish principle, fabricated a story improbable and inconsistent, which he thought would procure him a reward. Having probably witnessed the suicidal act of Saul, he thought of turning it to his own account, and suffered the penalty of his grievously mistaken calculation (compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.9">2Sa 1:9</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.4">1Sa 31:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.5">5</reference>). <div eID="gen3881" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c975e282efb8ba9fddae81dce786fbd0c28b393: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2828"/><div sID="gen3884" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2828"/><hi type="bold">13-15. David said unto the young man ... Whence art thou?--</hi>The man had at the outset stated who he was. But the question was now formally and judicially put. The punishment inflicted on the Amalekite may seem too severe, but the respect paid to kings in the West must not be regarded as the standard for that which the East may think due to royal station. David's reverence for Saul, as the Lord's anointed, was in his mind a principle on which he had faithfully acted on several occasions of great temptation. In present circumstances it was especially important that his principle should be publicly known; and to free himself from the imputation of being in any way accessory to the execrable crime of regicide was the part of a righteous judge, no less than of a good politician.<div eID="gen3884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3885" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.17-2Sam.1.27">2Sa 1:17-27</reference>. David Laments Saul and Jonathan. <div eID="gen3885" type="x-p"/>
entries.7aa81a8227fa8c1b71b54796752646c80a9417f3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2829"/><div sID="gen3886" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2829"/><hi type="bold">17-18. David lamented with this lamentation--</hi>It has always been customary for Eastern people, on the death of great kings and warriors, to celebrate their qualities and deeds in funeral songs. This inimitable pathetic elegy is supposed by many writers to have become a national war song, and to have been taught to the young Israelites under the name of "The Bow," in conformity with the practice of Hebrew and many classical writers in giving titles to their songs from the principal theme (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.1">Psa 22:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.56.1">56:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.60.1">60:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.80.1">80:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.100.1">100:1</reference>). Although the words "the use of" are a supplement by our translators, they may be rightly introduced, for the natural sense of this parenthetical verse is, that David took immediate measures for instructing the people in the knowledge and practice of archery, their great inferiority to the enemy in this military arm having been the main cause of the late national disaster. <div eID="gen3886" type="x-p"/>
entries.9319006280348e36d61a7ae1a34bd6450c1f61db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2830"/><div sID="gen3887" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2830"/><hi type="bold">19. The beauty of Israel is slain upon thy high places--</hi>literally, "the gazelle" or "antelope of Israel." In Eastern countries, that animal is the chosen type of beauty and symmetrical elegance of form.<div eID="gen3887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3888" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how are the mighty fallen!--</hi>This forms the chorus. <div eID="gen3888" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a8619b97e0d8bdc240368b37381ebcf89d55e6e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2831"/><div sID="gen3889" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2831"/><hi type="bold">21. let there be no dew, neither let there be rain--</hi>To be deprived of the genial atmospheric influences which, in those anciently cultivated hills, seem to have reared plenty of first-fruits in the corn harvests, was specified as the greatest calamity the lacerated feelings of the poet could imagine. The curse seems still to lie upon them; for the mountains of Gilboa are naked and sterile.<div eID="gen3889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3890" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the shield of the mighty is vilely cast away--</hi>To cast away the shield was counted a national disgrace. Yet, on that fatal battle of Gilboa, many of the Jewish soldiers, who had displayed unflinching valor in former battles, forgetful of their own reputation and their country's honor, threw away their shields and fled from the field. This dishonorable and cowardly conduct is alluded to with exquisitely touching pathos. <div eID="gen3890" type="x-p"/>
entries.4062a9b1c4e3dbdfcae0a756768f969a77b4a939: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2832"/><div sID="gen3891" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2832"/><hi type="bold">24-27. Ye daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you in scarlet, with other delights, &c.--</hi>The fondness for dress, which anciently distinguished Oriental women, is their characteristic still. It appears in their love of bright, gay, and divers colors, in profuse display of ornaments, and in various other forms. The inmost depths of the poet's feeling are stirred, and his amiable disposition appears in the strong desire to celebrate the good qualities of Saul, as well as Jonathan. But the praises of the latter form the burden of the poem, which begins and ends with that excellent prince. <chapter eID="2Sam.1"/>

entries.3aa9d029906896bf6f1a6c828f92f9c22d105211: <div eID="gen10641" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction to the Second Book of Samuel Otherwise Called the Second Book of the Kings</title> <div sID="gen10642" type="x-p"/> As this is a continuation of the preceding history, without any interruption, it can scarcely be called another book. Originally this and the preceding made but one book, and they have been separated without reason or necessity. For a general account of both, see the preface to the first book of Samuel. <div eID="gen10642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10643" type="x-p"/> It is generally allowed that this book comprehends a period of forty years, from about A.M. 2949 to 2989. See the prefixed chronological account. <div eID="gen10643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10644" type="x-p"/> It has been divided into three parts: in the first we have an account of the happy commencement of David's reign, 2 Samuel 1-10. In the second, David's unhappy fall, and its miserable consequences, 2 Samuel 11-18. In the third, his restoration to the Divine favor, the re-establishment of his kingdom, and the events which signalized the latter part of his reign, 2 Samuel 19-24. <div eID="gen10644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10645" type="x-p"/> An Amalekite comes to David, and informs him that the Philistines had routed the Israelites; and that Saul and his sons were slain, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.1-2Sam.1.4">2Sam 1:1-4</reference>. And pretends that he himself had despatched Saul, finding him ready to fall alive into the hands of the Philistines, and had brought his crown and bracelets to David, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.5-2Sam.1.10">2Sam 1:5-10</reference>. David and his men mourn for Saul and his sons, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.11">2Sam 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.12">2Sam 1:12</reference>. He orders the Amalekite, who professed that he had killed Saul, to be slain, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.13-2Sam.1.16">2Sam 1:13-16</reference>. David's funeral song for Saul and Jonathan, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.17-2Sam.1.27">2Sam 1:17-27</reference>.
entries.2ed15a49161e78c6473b1d701fe085de5837c6c6: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen10645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10646" type="x-p"/> A man came out of the camp - The whole account which this young man gives is a fabrication: in many of the particulars it is grossly self-contradictory. There is no fact in the case but the bringing of the crown, or diadem, and bracelets of Saul; which, as he appears to have been a plunderer of the slain, he found on the field of battle; and he brought them to David, and told the lie of having despatched Saul, merely to ingratiate himself with David.
entries.e5fcdf7133abfc17bd78f1b3a3dd8b6f20d44fd8: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen10646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10647" type="x-p"/> I am an Amalekite - Dr. Delaney remarks that an Amalekite took that crown from off the head of Saul, which he had forfeited by his disobedience in the case of Amalek.
entries.69532393711281facf136a4c3b11bec20192c23e: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen10647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10648" type="x-p"/> The crown - and the bracelet - The crown was probably no more than a royal fillet or diadem, both being the ensigns of royalty. It is sometimes customary in the East for a sovereign prince to give a crown and bracelets, when investing others with dominion or authority over certain provinces. Had Saul these in token of his being God's vicegerent, and that he held the kingdom from him alone?
entries.cbdb0a9ec45d49a41ab1050bab431a842147f67a: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen10648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10649" type="x-p"/> Thy blood be upon thy head - If he killed Saul, as he said he did, then he deserved death; at that time it was not known to the contrary, and this man was executed on his own confession.
entries.42fa8153fcd98fbc4a0844d6c727a807a28cf01b: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen10649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10650" type="x-p"/> David lamented - See this lamentation, and the notes on it at the end of this chapter, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.21">2Sam 1:21</reference> (note).
entries.8fe43f9758bdcf57402bb179591f265529eb6b1f: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen10650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10651" type="x-p"/> The use of the bow - The use of is not in the Hebrew; it is simply the bow, that is, a song thus entitled. See the observations at the end, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.21">2Sam 1:21</reference> (note).
entries.0a718e63a13f0b5f7f8d76973019139da40e34c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen10651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10652" type="x-p"/> As though he had not been - In stead of בלי beli, Not, I read כלי keley, Instruments. <div eID="gen10652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10653" type="x-p"/> Anointed with oil - See the observations at the end. <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.18">2Sam 1:18</reference>, etc.: He bade them teach the children of Judah the use of the bow, קשת kasheth. <div eID="gen10653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10654" type="x-p"/> The word kasheth is to be understood of the title of the song which immediately follows, and not of the use of the bow, as our translation intimates. <div eID="gen10654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10655" type="x-p"/> Many of David's Psalms have titles prefixed to them; some are termed Shosannim, some Maschil, Nehiloth, Neginoth, etc., and this one here, Kadesh or The Bow, because it was occasioned by the Philistine archers. <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.3">1Sam 31:3</reference> : "And the archers hit him." <div eID="gen10655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10656" type="x-p"/> But especially respecting the bow of Jonathan, "which returned not back from the blood of the slain," as the song itself expresses. And David could not but remember the bow of Jonathan, out of which "the arrow was shot beyond the lad," <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.36">1Sam 20:36</reference>. It was the time when that covenant was made, and that affection expressed between them "which was greater than the love of women." <div eID="gen10656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10657" type="x-p"/> On these accounts the song was entitled Kasheth, or The song of the Bow, and David commanded the chief musicians, Ethan, Heman, and Jeduthun, to teach the children of Judah to sing it. "It is written in the book of Jasher." Sept., επι βιβλιου του ευθους, "in the book of the upright." ספרא דאוריתא siphra deoraitha, "The book of the Law." - Jonathan. <div eID="gen10657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10658" type="x-p"/> The Arabic says, "Behold it is written in the book of Ashee; this is the book of Samuel;" the interpretation of which is, "book of songs or canticles." <div eID="gen10658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10659" type="x-p"/> This lamentation is justly admired as a picture of distress the most tender and the most striking; unequally divided by grief into longer and shorter breaks, as nature could pour them forth from a mind interrupted by the alternate recurrence of the most lively images of love and greatness. <div eID="gen10659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10660" type="x-p"/> His reverence for Saul and his love for Jonathan have their strongest colourings; but their greatness and bravery come full upon him, and are expressed with peculiar energy. <div eID="gen10660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10661" type="x-p"/> Being himself a warrior, it is in that character he sees their greatest excellence; and though his imagination hurries from one point of recollection to another, yet we hear him - at first, at last, everywhere - lamenting, How are the mighty fallen! <div eID="gen10661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10662" type="x-p"/> It is almost impossible to read the noble original without finding every word swollen with a sigh or broken with a sob. A heart pregnant with distress, and striving to utter expressions descriptive of its feelings, which are repeatedly interrupted by an excess of grief, is most sensibly painted throughout the whole. Even an English reader may be convinced of this, from the following specimen in European characters: - <div eID="gen10662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10663" type="x-p"/> 19. Hatstsebi Yishrael al bamotheycha chalal; Eych naphelu gibborim; <div eID="gen10663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10664" type="x-p"/> 20. Al taggidu begath, Al tebasseru bechutsoth Ashkelon; Pen tismachnah benoth Pelishtim, Pen taalozenah benoth haarelim. <div eID="gen10664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10665" type="x-p"/> 21. Harey baggilboa al tal, Veal matar aleychem usedey terumoth; Ki sham nigal magen Gibborim. Magen Shaul keley Mashiach bashshamen! <div eID="gen10665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10666" type="x-p"/> 22. Middam chalalim, mecheleb gibborim, Kesheth Yehonathan lo nashog achor; Vechereb Shaul lo thashub reykam. <div eID="gen10666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10667" type="x-p"/> 23. Shaul Vihonathan, Hannee habim vehanneimim bechaiyeyhem, Ubemotham lo niphradu. Minnesharim kallu, mearayoth gaberu! <div eID="gen10667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10668" type="x-p"/> 24. Benoth Yishrael el Shaul becheynah; Hammalbishchem shani im adanim, Hammaaleh adi zahab al lebushechen. <div eID="gen10668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10669" type="x-p"/> 25. Eych naphelu gibborim bethoch hammilchamah! Yehonathan al bamotheycha chalal! <div eID="gen10669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10670" type="x-p"/> 26. Tsar li aleycha achi Yehonathan, naamta li meod Niphleathah ahabathecha li meahabath nashim! <div eID="gen10670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10671" type="x-p"/> 27.
